messages.subject: Nominal Response Model from BUGS - (slow code)
parts:
Hello!

I am relatively new to STAN, so bear with me.

I'm trying to translate a Nominal Response model (Bock 1972) from a working BUGS code that runs interminably slowly.  I've tried STAN with the same code, but the performance fares equally as poorly, if not worse, which leads me to suspect I'm doing something suboptimal in the world of STAN, but have had no luck in figuring it out over the course of a day of putzing.

My primary thought is that (from forums and such):

resp[k,j]'~categorical(p[j,k]);

should be done all at once as vectors.  That's fine, but I run across an error when I form it as resp'<-categorical(p): 

no matches for function name="transpose"
    arg 0 type=int[2]
available function signatures for transpose:
0.  transpose(vector) : row vector
1.  transpose(row vector) : vector
2.  transpose(matrix) : matrix
expression is ill formed


Probably something painfully simple that I've been unable to uncover or a gap in my understanding.  Thanks for any input.

Best,
Par Jason Engle

---------------------------------

data{
int N;
int T;
int NC;
int resp[T,N];
real lam[T,NC];
}

parameters{
real theta[N];
real thetaN[T];
matrix[T,NC] z;
}

model
{
vector[NC] tt[N,T];
vector[NC] p[N,T];
matrix[N,T] sumtt;

// Nominal model  - Bock 1972

// iterate over respondents
for (j in 1:N) {
//Iterate over items
for (k in 1:T) {
// Iterate over categories
for (l in 1:10) {
tt[j,k,l]<- exp(z[k,l]+lam[k,l]*(fabs(theta[j]-thetaN[k])));
}
sumtt[j,k]<-tt[j,k,1]+tt[j,k,2]+tt[j,k,3]+tt[j,k,4]+tt[j,k,5]+tt[j,k,6]+tt[j,k,7]+tt[j,k,8]+tt[j,k,9]+tt[j,k,10];
}
}

// iterate over respondents
for (j in 1:N) {
//Iterate over items
for (k in 1:T) {
// Iterate over categories
for (l in 1:10) {
p[j,k,l]<-tt[j,k,l]/sumtt[j,k];
}}}


//Iterate over items
for (j in 1:N) {
for (k in 1:T) {
resp[k,j]'~categorical(p[j,k]);
}
}

//Iterate over items
for (k in 1:T) {
// Iterate over categories
for (l in 1:10) {
z[k,l]~normal(0,1);
}
}

theta~normal(0,1);
thetaN~normal(0,1);

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Nominal Response Model from BUGS - (slow code)
parts:
On 1/21/14, 3:33 PM, Jason Engle wrote:

> I'm trying to translate a Nominal Response model (Bock 1972) from a working BUGS code that runs interminably slowly.
> I've tried STAN with the same code, but the performance fares equally as poorly, if not worse,

Is it mixing slowly or just running slowly per iteration?
Speeding up the implementation won't help with the mixing.
Often poor mixing arises because a model's not well identified.

What you want to compare is time per effective sample, not
time per iteration. The number of effective samples you get out
in the end is all that matters in terms of posterior inference.
The residual error in estimating posterior means is reported
as MCMC std error in Stan output, and that's just (estimated)
posterior variance divided by the sqrt of the number of effective
samples.

> which leads me to suspect
> I'm doing something suboptimal in the world of STAN, but have had no luck in figuring it out over the course of a day of
> putzing.

> My primary thought is that (from forums and such):
>
> resp[k,j]'~categorical(p[j,k]);
>
> should be done all at once as vectors. That's fine, but I run across an error when I form it as resp'<-categorical(p):
>
> no matches for function name="transpose"
> arg 0 type=int[2]
> available function signatures for transpose:
> 0. transpose(vector) : row vector
> 1. transpose(row vector) : vector
> 2. transpose(matrix) : matrix
> expression is ill formed

Stan's strongly typed and each function is very picky about
the type of arguments it works on. Your variable "resp"
is a 2D integer array (i.e., int[2]), whereas the transpose
operator (') only applies to vectors, row vectors, or matrices.

I rewrote the model for you more efficiently. To understand
the changes, note that if x is a matrix then x[n] is a row
vector, and look up the definition of categorical_logit, which
will lead you to softmax. You were implementing softmax yourself
in code. But using the correct parameterization of categorical
will be much faster. Also note that I vectorized the prior for z.

And please check my work on the transforms
to make sure that both I did it right and you understand what I did.
(We should have a version of categorical_logit that takes a row vector
as a parameter, and then you wouldn't need that final transposition.)

You could definite temporaries for the argument to categorical_logit,
but it's not necessary in Stan.

- Bob

data {
int N;
int T;
int NC;
int resp[T,N];
matrix[T,NC] lam;

}
parameters {
real theta[N];
real thetaN[T];
matrix[T,NC] z;
}
model {

theta ~ normal(0,1);
thetaN ~ normal(0,1);

for (t in 1:T)
z[t] ~ normal(0,1);

for (n in 1:N)
for (t in 1:T)
resp[t,n] ~ categorical_logit((z[t]
+ lam[t] * fabs(theta[n] - thetaN[t]))');
}

Andrew's always hung up the lexicon, even though
I'm the linguist in the group.

We haven't had any problem getting IRT models to mix
and sample well, even at large scale.

The best thing you can do if the model's not well
identified (often the problem with correlated parameters)
is come up with some kind of reparameterization that is
well identified. But keep in mind it has to be well
identified on the unconstrained scale for really
optimal behavior, though you can often get better mixing
in practice if you just define some transformed parameters
or generated quantities of interest that are identified.

Our multivariate distributions like categorical_logit
aren't vectorized, so you're not going to have luck
there. The categorical_logit will should make things a lot
faster compared to your computing softmax yourself in
Stan code --- it precomputes all the derivatives rather
than figuring them all out with the chain rule at run time.
The other vectorization shouldn't make much of a difference
other than simplifying the code.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Nominal Response Model from BUGS - (slow code)
parts:
There are several ways you can identify a model like this.
But they'll all be pretty ugly to code in Stan as is.

What we really need is a mean_zero vector data type (a K-vector
gets K-1 free parameters). And a first_element_zero vector data type
(also K-1 free params). In the meantime...

One approach is to define each row as a scaled and offset
simplex:

parameters {
simplex[NC] z_raw[T];
real<lower=0> z_scale[T];
...
}
transformed parameters {
matrix[T,NC] z;
...
for (t in 1:T)

z[t] <- z_scale[t] * (z_raw[t] - 1.0 / T);

...
}

This lets the z be anything but insures each z[t] sums to 0.
You then want to define priors on the z_raw (perhaps uniform)
and on the z_scale (whatever makes sense).

The other standard approach is to fix one of the values in each
row, such as z[t,1] == 0. To do this, you need to define (NC-1)-vectors
that are free, then put them back together in z. Not very pretty.
And also asymmetric in terms of the priors.

To constrain the sign of just one entry in an M-vector, you have
to define it like this:

parameters {
vector[M-1] a2_M;
real<lower=0> a1;
}
transformed parameters {
vector[M] a;
a[1] <- a1;
for (m in 2:M)
a[m] <- a2_M[m-1];
}

File this under "stupid Stan tricks" :-)

- Bob

messages.subject: additive redundant parameterization to handle nonidentifiability
parts:
There's also the post processing trick, which goes as follows:

Suppose you have parameters theta_1,…,theta_J whose overall level is nonidentified jointly with some other parameter. For example, there is a term in the model, mu + theta_j, and the likelihood is unchanged if you add a const to mu and subtract that const from the vector theta.

You get identification in two steps:
(1) Assign weak priors to the theta_j's, just so they have a proper posterior. For example, independent normal priors with mean 0 and scale 10.
(2) Create derived parameters:
mu.adj <- mu + mean(theta)
theta.adj_j <- theta_j - mean(theta).
You run the HMC on (mu,theta), but you save and monitor convergence of (mu.adj, theta.adj).
This is what we call the additive redundant parameterization in the ARM book.

Ideally this could be done in a more automatic way (I think this might be what Bob is saying when he is talking about a mean_zero vector data type). As it is, it's a bit of a hack because you have to define these additive parameters manually. But it can work.

parts:
Michael should weigh in here, but I don't think the post-processing
trick is a great idea with our adaptive HMC, because it's not
where the sampling will happen. We'd rather have the parameters
defined in the parameters block be well identified.

If someone wants to actually evaluate both options empirically,
that'd be great (and it'd be a paper, as Andrew likes to say).

- Bob

> There's also the post processing trick, which goes as follows:

> Suppose you have parameters theta_1,…,theta_J whose overall level is nonidentified jointly with some other parameter. For example, there is a term in the model, mu + theta_j, and the likelihood is unchanged if you add a const to mu and subtract that const from the vector theta.
>
> You get identification in two steps:
> (1) Assign weak priors to the theta_j's, just so they have a proper posterior. For example, independent normal priors with mean 0 and scale 10.
> (2) Create derived parameters:
> mu.adj <- mu + mean(theta)
> theta.adj_j <- theta_j - mean(theta).
> You run the HMC on (mu,theta), but you save and monitor convergence of (mu.adj, theta.adj).
> This is what we call the additive redundant parameterization in the ARM book.
>

Again, thanks.  All this is not to say that this isn't possible.  By all accounts it should be with some coaxing.
